packet.description_seed: Chiefs in Ontario say they were left to self-evacuate before homes burned to ground, after being told there was no imminent threat Fast-moving wildfires have burned two First Nations communities in Canada to the ground, as members said they were left to self-evacuate without government help or emergency alerts. Chiefs in Ontario say they were left to self-evacuate before homes burned to ground, after being told there was no imminent threat Fast-moving wildfires have burned two First Nations communities in Canada to the ground, as members said they were left to self-evacuate without government help or emergency alerts. Thirteen communities in Ontario province have been ordered to evacuate because of wildfires, most of them First Nations. The Ontario premier, Doug Ford, told reporters on Monday that close to 2,000 people had been evacuated so far to cities including Toronto and Niagara Falls. There are nearly 1,000 wildfires burning across Canada, with about 200 in Ontario. The prime minister, Mark Carney, said heatwaves and dry weather had combined to create “one of the most intense wildfire seasons in Canadian history”.

Ford travelled to Thunder Bay over the weekend and said the province was willing to spend whatever was necessary to fight the fires. However, First Nations leaders, including from the Anishinabek Nation, accused the premier of being unclear about what support the province was providing and, and of disorganisation in coordinating with First Nations. The CBC has reported that although Ontario spent $271m on emergency firefighting in 2025-26, it plans to spend only $150m in 2026-27. The Ontario government did not respond to requests for comment. First Nations communities are acutely vulnerable to wildfire danger in Canada, with 80% of Indigenous communities located in areas more susceptible to fires, according to a 2019 study from ---

Namaygoosisagagun First Nation, located north of Thunder Bay in north-western Ontario, was engulfed by fire on 15 June. About two dozen people quickly boarded boats packed with their possessions and raced across the nearby lake. “If this community waited for a mandatory evacuation process, we’d be doing a recovery mission for the bodies of children, of elders, of men and women,” said Linda Debassige, grand council chief of the Anishinabek Nation, which represents 39 Ontario First Nations. All members safely escaped but the community’s buildings and other infrastructure were completely destroyed. The Namaygoosisagagun people evacuated to Thunder Bay, where the Anishinabek Nation has been providing assistance. Debassige said that Namaygoosisagagun’s chief, Helen Paavola, had made inquiries to the federal government in the days leading up to the fire, but the community had been assured there was no imminent threat.

Fast-moving wildfires have burned two First Nations communities in Canada to the ground, as members said they were left to self-evacuate without government help or emergency alerts.

Thirteen communities in Ontario province have been ordered to evacuate because of wildfires, most of them First Nations. The Ontario premier, Doug Ford, told reporters on Monday that close to 2,000 people had been evacuated so far to cities including Toronto and Niagara Falls.

There are nearly 1,000 wildfires burning across Canada, with about 200 in Ontario. The prime minister, Mark Carney, said heatwaves and dry weather had combined to create “one of the most intense wildfire seasons in Canadian history”.

Namaygoosisagagun First Nation, located north of Thunder Bay in north-western Ontario, was engulfed by fire on 15 June. About two dozen people quickly boarded boats packed with their possessions and raced across the nearby lake.

“If this community waited for a mandatory evacuation process, we’d be doing a recovery mission for the bodies of children, of elders, of men and women,” said Linda Debassige, grand council chief of the Anishinabek Nation, which represents 39 Ontario First Nations.

All members safely escaped but the community’s buildings and other infrastructure were completely destroyed. The Namaygoosisagagun people evacuated to Thunder Bay, where the Anishinabek Nation has been providing assistance.

Debassige said that Namaygoosisagagun’s chief, Helen Paavola, had made inquiries to the federal government in the days leading up to the fire, but the community had been assured there was no imminent threat.

Ford travelled to Thunder Bay over the weekend and said the province was willing to spend whatever was necessary to fight the fires.

However, First Nations leaders, including from the Anishinabek Nation, accused the premier of being unclear about what support the province was providing and, and of disorganisation in coordinating with First Nations.

The Ontario government did not respond to requests for comment.

This story is published through the Indigenous News Alliance.

In April, when an out-of-control wildfire threatened the remote Xeni Gwet’in First Nation in western Canada, local governments issued evacuation alerts. The blaze quickly spread to 618 acres before being extinguished a few days later, and people were allowed to return home.

Although the nearly 500 residents of Xeni Gwet’in were relieved, the crisis provided a reminder of what many Indigenous leaders say is Canada’s inadequate emergency communications with their communities. Authorities do not provide alerts in the Tŝilhqot’in language, the only one spoken by many elders in Xeni Gwet’in, and the mother tongue of nearly 650 people in the larger Tŝilhqot’in Nation. This adds an additional challenge during disasters because many families rely on them to make decisions in important moments.

“Our elders are who we look to for support,” said Chantu William, who is Tsilhqot’in and a youth policy program development coordinator in Xeni Gwet’in. William said that the nation’s forestry crew must alert them directly.

This community-led approach is not always enough during larger disasters, and Indigenous peoples are left waiting for emergency services to respond. “It would be nice if we had those preventative things on our own already,” William said.

At the United Nations Expert Mechanism on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, or EMRIP, which is meeting in Geneva this week, inadequate resources, poor communication, and unsafe conditions were common grievances among Indigenous delegates. The stakes grow increasingly dire as climate change makes natural disasters like wildfires, floods, and extreme weather more common and more intense. Delegates are urging local and national authorities to consult directly with them to better protect Indigenous lives and lands from the ravages of a warming world. To Indigenous peoples, climate disaster and conflict are linked symptoms of colonialism.

In response to this growing problem, EMRIP embarked on a study to understand the issue. A draft of that research, based on more than 80 submissions from states, national human rights institutions, Indigenous people, and non-governmental organizations, was presented in Geneva this week. As an out-of-control wildfire tore through Namaygoosisagagun First Nation, also known as Collins First Nation, residents grabbed what they could and escaped in boats with flames burning behind them. Others fled with only the clothes on their backs. By the time the smoke cleared, much of the remote community about 210 kilometres north of Thunder Bay had been destroyed.

The harrowing escape has become one of the defining images of Ontario's rapidly escalating wildfire emergency. But Nishnawbe Aski Nation Grand Chief Alvin Fiddler says Collins is far from the only community living through devastation.

"Our hearts are with the leadership there and the people, and we're thankful that everyone got out safely," Fiddler told Yahoo News Canada.

"Tragically, everything is gone in their community. There is nothing left there."

payload.title: Kanadan maastopalot tuhosivat kaksi alkuperäiskansojen yhteisöä
payload.summary: Ontarion alkuperäiskansojen johtajat arvostelevat viranomaisia puutteellisista varoituksista ja evakuointiavusta nopeasti levinneiden maastopalojen keskellä.
payload.content:
Kanadan Ontariossa nopeasti edenneet maastopalot ovat tuhonneet kaksi alkuperäiskansojen yhteisöä. Yhteisöjen jäsenet ja johtajat arvostelevat viranomaisten toimintaa, sillä heidän mukaansa asukkaat joutuivat lähtemään omin voimin ilman hallituksen apua tai hätävaroituksia.

## Asukkaat pakenivat järven yli

Thunder Bayn pohjoispuolella sijaitseva Namaygoosisagagun First Nation jäi palon saartamaksi 15. kesäkuuta. Noin kaksikymmentä ihmistä pakkasi omaisuuttaan veneisiin ja pakeni läheisen järven yli tulen edetessä kohti yhteisöä.

Kaikki asukkaat pääsivät turvaan, mutta yhteisön rakennukset ja muu infrastruktuuri tuhoutuivat kokonaan. Evakuoidut siirtyivät Thunder Bayhin, missä 39:ää Ontarion alkuperäiskansojen yhteisöä edustava Anishinabek Nation on järjestänyt heille apua.

Anishinabek Nationin johtaja Linda Debassigen mukaan pakollisen evakuoinnin odottaminen olisi voinut johtaa kuolonuhreihin. Hän kertoi Namaygoosisagagunin johtajan Helen Paavolan tiedustelleen vaarasta liittovaltiolta paloa edeltäneinä päivinä. Yhteisölle oli kuitenkin vakuutettu, ettei välitöntä uhkaa ollut.

## Lähes 2 000 ihmistä evakuoitu

Ontariossa 13 yhteisöä on määrätty evakuoitaviksi maastopalojen vuoksi. Suurin osa niistä on alkuperäiskansojen yhteisöjä. Provinssin pääministeri Doug Ford sanoi maanantaina, että lähes 2 000 ihmistä oli siirretty muun muassa Torontoon ja Niagara Fallsiin.

Kanadassa palaa kaikkiaan lähes tuhat maastopaloa, joista noin 200 Ontariossa. Pääministeri Mark Carney on kuvaillut kuluvaa kautta yhdeksi Kanadan historian voimakkaimmista maastopalokausista. Hänen mukaansa tilannetta ovat pahentaneet helleaallot ja kuiva sää.

## Alkuperäiskansojen johtajat vaativat selkeyttä

Ford vieraili viikonloppuna Thunder Bayssa ja vakuutti Ontarion käyttävän palontorjuntaan niin paljon rahaa kuin tarvitaan. Anishinabek Nationin ja muiden alkuperäiskansojen johtajat ovat kuitenkin arvostelleet provinssia epäselvistä tukitoimista ja puutteellisesta yhteistyön koordinoinnista.

Kanadan yleisradioyhtiö CBC:n mukaan Ontario käytti vuosina 2025–2026 hätätilanteiden palontorjuntaan 271 miljoonaa dollaria. Vuosille 2026–2027 menoja on suunniteltu 150 miljoonaa dollaria. Ontarion hallitus ei vastannut sille esitettyihin kommenttipyyntöihin.
summary_bullets: Kaksi alkuperäiskansojen yhteisöä on tuhoutunut Ontarion maastopaloissa.
Lähes 2 000 ihmistä on evakuoitu, ja evakuointimääräys koskee 13:a yhteisöä.
Alkuperäiskansojen johtajat arvostelevat viranomaisten varoituksia, tukitoimia ja koordinointia.
payload.journalist_note: Keskeiset tapahtumat ja luvut ovat yhden kansainvälisen uutisraportin varassa. Ontarion hallituksen vastausta esitettyyn arvosteluun ei ollut saatavilla.

Ford vieraili viikonloppuna Thunder Bayssa ja vakuutti Ontarion käyttävän palontorjuntaan niin paljon rahaa kuin tarvitaan. Anishinabek Nationin ja muiden alkuperäiskansojen johtajat ovat kuitenkin arvostelleet provinssia epäselvistä tukitoimista ja puutteellisesta yhteistyön koordinoinnista.

Kanadan yleisradioyhtiö CBC:n mukaan Ontario käytti vuosina 2025–2026 hätätilanteiden palontorjuntaan 271 miljoonaa dollaria. Vuosille 2026–2027 menoja on suunniteltu 150 miljoonaa dollaria. Ontarion hallitus ei vastannut sille esitettyihin kommenttipyyntöihin.

Chiefs in Ontario say they were left to self-evacuate before homes burned to ground, after being told there was no imminent threat Fast-moving wildfires have burned two First Nations communities in Canada to the ground, as members said they were left to self-evacuate without government help or emergency alerts. Thirteen communities in Ontario province have been ordered to evacuate because of wildfires, most of them First Nations. The Ontario premier, Doug Ford, told reporters on Monday that close to 2,000 people had been evacuated so far to cities including Toronto and Niagara Falls. There are nearly 1,000 wildfires burning across Canada, with about 200 in Ontario. The prime minister, Mark Carney, said heatwaves and dry weather had combined to create “one of the most intense wildfire seasons in Canadian history”.

Ford travelled to Thunder Bay over the weekend and said the province was willing to spend whatever was necessary to fight the fires. However, First Nations leaders, including from the Anishinabek Nation, accused the premier of being unclear about what support the province was providing and, and of disorganisation in coordinating with First Nations. The CBC has reported that although Ontario spent $271m on emergency firefighting in 2025-26, it plans to spend only $150m in 2026-27. The Ontario government did not respond to requests for comment. First Nations communities are acutely vulnerable to wildfire danger in Canada, with 80% of Indigenous communities located in areas more susceptible to fires, according to a 2019 study from ---

Namaygoosisagagun First Nation, located north of Thunder Bay in north-western Ontario, was engulfed by fire on 15 June. About two dozen people quickly boarded boats packed with their possessions and raced across the nearby lake. “If this community waited for a mandatory evacuation process, we’d be doing a recovery mission for the bodies of children, of elders, of men and women,” said Linda Debassige, grand council chief of the Anishinabek Nation, which represents 39 Ontario First Nations. All members safely escaped but the community’s buildings and other infrastructure were completely destroyed. The Namaygoosisagagun people evacuated to Thunder Bay, where the Anishinabek Nation has been providing assistance. Debassige said that Namaygoosisagagun’s chief, Helen Paavola, had made inquiries to the federal government in the days leading up to the fire, but the community had been assured there was no imminent threat.
